In this case, the patient had no specific treatment needs related to withdrawal. Given these findings, the patient met ASAM 3.1 requirements for this dimension.For dimension 2, the patient’s biomedical conditions, including physical health concerns, should be discussed and scored. In this case, the patient’s biomedical problems were stable and did not require medical or nurse monitoring, and the patient was capable of self-administering any prescribed medication. The patient had no specific treatment needs related to physical health concerns. Given these findings, the patient met ASAM 3.1 requirements for this dimension.For dimension 3, the patient’s psychiatric and cognitive conditions and history, including active psychiatric symptoms and persistent disability should be discussed and scored. In this case, the patient struggled with serious persecutory delusions and ideas of reference and grandeur. This impaired his reality testing and his ability to participate in his aftercare and discharge planning process rationally and objectively. His psychiatric condition required ongoing treatment, but the patient was extremely resistant to starting medication because of side effects and difficulty trusting previous treatment teams. Overall, the patient’s co-occurring psychiatric condition was being addressed concurrently through appropriate psychiatric services. Given these findings, the patient met ASAM 3.1 requirements for this dimension.For dimension 4, the patient’s substance use-related risks, including the likelihood of engaging in risky substance use and the likelihood of engaging in risky substance use disorder-related behaviors should be discussed and scored. In this case, the patient understood the significance of relapse but did not appear to demonstrate the skills to be able to stay sober outside of a structured and supervised setting. He had an unstable and poorly treated psychiatric condition, which would predictably get worse with the reinstatement of some of the drugs of his choice, including amphetamines, cannabinoids, alcohol, and opioids. The likelihood of risky substance use remained at least moderate. However, the consequences of substance use with this underlying psychiatric diagnosis created further unpredictability and an additional risk to the patient and to the community. Given these findings, the patient met ASAM 3.1 requirements for this dimension.For dimension 5, the patient’s recovery environment interactions, including the ability to function effectively in the current environment, safety in the current environment, and support in the current environment should be discussed and scored. The patient demonstrates incomplete engagement and an ambivalent, avoidant, or distrustful relationship with clinicians and other care providers. Thus, the patient has a total score of 16. Therefore, intensive outpatient program services were not and are not medically necessary for the treatment of this patient. Final Result: The reviewer determined that the services at issue were not and are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. Study criteria focuses on six dimensions to determine the appropriate level of care, which includes: (1) intoxication and associated risk, withdrawal and associated risks, and addiction medication needs; (2) biomedical conditions including physical health concerns and pregnancy-related concerns; (3) psychiatric and cognitive conditions and history including active psychiatric symptoms and persistent disability; (4) substance use-related risks including the likelihood of engaging in risky substance use and the likelihood of engaging in risky substance use disorder-related behaviors; (5) recovery environment interactions including the ability to function effectively in the current environment, safety in the current environment, and support in the current environment; and (6) patient-centered considerations including barriers to care, patient preferences, and the need for motivational enhancement.For dimension 1, the patient’s intoxication and associated risk, withdrawal and associated risks, and addiction medication needs should be discussed and scored. In this case, the patient was not intoxicated upon admission, but his urine drug screen (UTOX) was positive for alcohol, amphetamine, buprenorphine, cocaine, and methamphetamine. He was therefore placed on medications for detoxification. Given these findings, the patient met study requirements for this dimension.For dimension 2, the patient’s biomedical conditions, including physical health concerns should be discussed and scored. In this case, the patient had no acute medical problems during his RTC stay that interfered with his treatment. He was seen prior to admission at a hospital for syncope, but he was cleared and released and was told it was the result of using alcohol and drugs. Given these findings, the patient met requirements for this dimension.For dimension 3, the patient’s psychiatric and cognitive conditions and history, including active psychiatric symptoms and persistent disability should be discussed and scored. In this case, the patient had a history of being treated for anxiety and attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD). He reported that he had his first panic attack in childhood and reported he has had a few panic attacks since admission to the RTC. He also reported overthinking things and lacking the motivation to do things. The patient was evaluated by a psychologist who felt that the patient needed more clean time to work on his mental health issues. The patient’s mental status was described as slowed motor activity, pressured speech, intense eye contact, flat affect, circumstantial thoughts, guarded behavior, and poor insight and judgement. Given these findings, the patient met the requirements for this dimension.For dimension 4, the patient’s substance use-related risks, including the likelihood of engaging in risky substance use and the likelihood of engaging in risky substance use disorder-related behaviors should be discussed and scored. In this case, the patient had a history of several high-risk behaviors, including being in bad neighborhoods, driving under the influence, infidelity under the influence, lying, having multiple sexual partners, overspending, poor decision making, poor diet, poor health, sexual promiscuity, stealing, and using substances at work. The patient had been arrested on alcohol-related charges in the past. Given these findings, the patient met the requirements for this dimension.For dimension 5, the patient’s recovery environment interactions, including the ability to function effectively in the current environment, safety in the current environment, and support in the current environment should be discussed and scored. In this case, the patient had previously left sober living and relapsed. He had no job and had a very poor financial situation, along with being a chronic relapser. The patient was unlikely to follow up with outpatient treatment and had changed his mind about going to sober living. Given these findings, the patient met the requirements for this dimension.For dimension 6, the patient’s barriers to care, patient preferences, and need for motivational enhancement should be considered. In this case, the patient had a history of chronically relapsing. He had been to this RTC a total of six times. He reported at least ten attempts at sobriety in the past and relapsed every time. He reported that he wants to get his own place, get a good job, stay sober, and find his purpose in life.Using the criteria, this patient met all dimensional criteria for medical necessity and therefore qualified for the treatment for the time period under review. In addition, the RTC services were in accordance with the generally accepted standards of mental health and substance use disorder care, clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration, and not were medically necessary for the treatment of this patient.Final Result: The reviewer determined that the services at issue were medically necessary for the treatment of the patient’s medical condition. Therefore, the Health Plan’s denial should be overturned.Credentials/Qualifications: The reviewer is board certified in psychiatry with subspecialty certification in addiction medicine and is actively practicing. The reviewer is an expert in the treatment of the enrollee’s medical condition and knowledgeable about the proposed treatment through recent or current actual clinical experience treating those with the same or a similar medical condition.

Findings:  The physician reviewer found that Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: The patient has requested authorization and coverage for electroconvulsive therapy (ECT). The records indicate that this patient’s condition is most accurately described as alcohol use disorder, severe. He does not yet meet the criteria for early remission, which requires at least three months of no symptoms except for cravings. This means that the patient is currently in the phase of recovery that is most susceptible to relapse, which could potentially predispose him to prolonged seizures during ECT. Moreover, alcohol is a depressant, so the patient should attain a period of sobriety of at least three months in order to determine whether depressive symptoms more fully remit in the absence of alcohol prior to attempted treatment with ECT. He has been unable to tolerate trials of two different antidepressants, although much of the trial period overlapped with active alcohol use. Overall, ECT is considered a treatment for patients with treatment-resistant depression. However, this patient has not undergone adequate trials of antidepressant medications during sobriety to determine whether he is likely to respond to treatment with medications. Furthermore, there is a lack of details with regard to the nature and severity of the patient’s traumatic brain injury (TBI) to help determine the patient’s risk of seizure with ECT. Given the patient’s history of repeated relapse, less than 90 days of sobriety, and history of TBI, the use of ECT is not recommended. For these reasons, the requested ECT is not medically necessary for the treatment of this patient. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: The patient has requested reimbursement for residential treatment center (RTC) services. The American Association of Community Psychiatrists Level of Care Utilization System (LOCUS) provides a reliable framework for determining the appropriate level of care for adults needing mental health treatment. Using LOCUS, providers score patients on a scale of 1-5 using a six-pronged Dimensional Rating System. The six dimensions include: (1) risk of harm; (2) functional status; (3) medical, addictive and psychiatric comorbidity; (4) recovery environment (a. stressors and b. supports); (5) treatment and recovery history; and (6) engagement. The composite score is then used to determine the level of care needed. Applying the LOCUS framework, the patient met the criteria for RTC services.For dimension 1, the patient had a moderate risk of harm (score 3) due to the patient’s history of chronic and impulsive suicidal threats. The patient was endorsing worsening suicidal ideation during the period under review, with the intention to act on these thoughts by stealing a knife or overdosing. There was also evidence of self-neglect and decreasing ability of the patient to care for himself in the current environment, given his food-restricting behaviors.For dimension 2, the patient demonstrated serious functional impairment (score 4). The records note that the patient was increasingly withdrawn and isolated while in the RTC program. He was not meeting his nutritional goals at the standards that were set for him. The patient also reported some interpersonal struggles, including “lying” behaviors and not feeling honest with clinicians.For dimension 3, the patient had significant co-morbidities (score 3). The patient’s eating disorder was a significant concern for the treating clinicians, as it was exacerbating his symptoms. The patient’s depression and suicidal ideation required frequent and urgent on-call physician consultation, demonstrating acute exacerbations of psychiatric symptoms that seriously impaired his ability to function at those times. Thus, medical conditions existed which adversely affected the course of the presenting disorder. For dimension 4A, the patient’s recovery environment was mildly stressful (score 2). The records indicate that the patient was undergoing significant transitions from home to university life, as well as a breakup with his girlfriend. The patient reported ongoing concern about his ability to be successful or improve in his depressive symptoms. As such, there were transitions requiring adjustments such as a change in household members or a new job or school. For dimension 4B, the patient’s recovery environment was supportive (score 2). Based on the records, the patient appeared to have supportive caregivers. Accordingly, some elements of the support system were willing and able to participate in treatment if requested to do so and had the capacity to effect needed changes. For dimension 5, the patient showed poor response to treatment and recovery management (score 4). The patient previously participated in various levels of ambulatory treatment, including outpatient therapy and medication management services, intensive outpatient program (IOP), and partial hospitalization program (PHP)-level care, prior to RTC. Notably, due to his active eating disorder, the patient was declined outpatient treatment and instead referred to eating disorder-specific PHP treatment, prior to stepping up to RTC services. Previous or current treatment had not achieved complete remission of symptoms or optimal control of symptoms even with intensive and/or repeated exposure. For dimension 6, the patient exhibited limited engagement and recovery (score 3). The patient expressed frequent frustration with his diagnosis and ability to improve. He was also noted to withhold information related to his treatment from treating providers. Overall, the patient related to treatment with some difficulty and established few, if any, trusting relationships. These findings give the patient a composite score of 21, which is consistent with medically monitored non-residential services. However, the patient’s score of 4 under functional impairment supports the patient’s placement in medically monitored residential services or RTC for the period under review. Furthermore, RTC services were in accordance with the generally accepted standards of mental health and substance use disorder care, clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration, and not primarily for the convenience of the patient or provider. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: The patient has requested authorization and coverage for Wegovy. Obesity is a disease associated with a significant increase in mortality and many health risks, including type 2 diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, and coronary heart disease. Weight loss in patients with obesity is associated with a reduction in mortality. Clinical guidelines for the medical care of patients with obesity report that patients with obesity should be considered for treatment with weight-loss medication combined with lifestyle therapy when necessary. Bray and colleagues state, “For patients who struggle with weight loss and who would receive health benefits from weight loss, management of medications that are contributing to weight gain and use of approved medications for chronic weight management along with lifestyle changes are appropriate.” Medications for weight loss are generally considered an option for patients with a body mass index (BMI) greater than 27 kg/m² with comorbidities such as diabetes or sleep apnea, or with a BMI greater than 30 kg/m² without comorbidities. Medications approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) for the treatment of obesity include orlistat, naltrexone-bupropion, phentermine, phentermine with topiramate, liraglutide, and semaglutide. Semaglutide (brand name Wegovy) has demonstrated impressive efficacy in weight reduction. In a study examining the effects of semaglutide versus placebo, researchers report that the mean change in body weight from baseline to week 68 was a 14.9% decrease in the semaglutide group as compared with a 2.4% decrease in the placebo group. The authors noted, “participants who received semaglutide had a greater improvement with respect to cardiometabolic risk factors and a greater increase in participant-reported physical functioning from baseline than those who received placebo.” In a 52-week placebo-controlled clinical trial comparing the benefits of semaglutide with liraglutide and placebo, researchers reported that for patients receiving 0.2 mg or more of semaglutide daily, combined with diet and exercise modification, there was dose-dependent, clinically relevant weight loss that was significantly greater than placebo at all tested doses, and higher than those taking liraglutide 3.0 mg daily. In this case, the patient has obesity, with a BMI of 35 kg/m². While lifestyle interventions such as diet and exercise represent the cornerstone of weight management, as the patient has been unsuccessful in losing weight despite six months of lifestyle changes, the provider has prescribed Wegovy. Using LOCUS, providers score patients on a scale of 1-5 using a six-pronged Dimensional Rating System. The six dimensions include: (1) risk of harm; (2) functional status; (3) medical, addictive and psychiatric comorbidity; (4) recovery environment (a. stressors and b. supports); (5) treatment and recovery history; and (6) engagement. The composite score is then used to determine the level of care needed. Applying the LOCUS framework, this patient meets the criteria for RTC services, and fewer than 30 hours per week of ERP therapy in the RTC setting. For dimension 1, the patient has been at moderate risk of harm (score 3) due to a lack of current suicidal or homicidal ideation. However, the patient reportedly had transient suicidal thoughts in the past. The patient also has a history of a substance use disorder but no recent use. The patient has some evidence of decreased ability to properly care for himself in his current environment. For dimension 2, the patient has shown serious functional impairment (score 4) given his significant withdrawal and avoidance of all social interactions as well as serious disturbances in physical functioning including weight loss. The patient has been unable to work or fulfill other obligations on a frequent basis for an extended period of time. For dimension 3, the patient has significant co-morbidity (score 3) considering his OCD, poor eating habits, and weight loss which place him at risk of developing medical conditions. The patient has significant psychiatric symptoms which are debilitating and have an adverse effect on the severity of his co-occurring substance use disorder, in the setting of no recent use. For dimension 4A, the patient’s recovery environment has been moderately stressful (score 3) due to his inability to work since he lost his job two years ago. The patient has experienced deterioration of interpersonal relationships due to his condition. For dimension 4B, the patient’s recovery environment has provided limited support (score 3). The provider noted that the patient has few supportive resources in his current environment as the closest PHP that provides ERP is reportedly three hours away from his residence. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: The patient has requested reimbursement for residential treatment center (RTC) services (ASAM 3.1). Per American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) criteria, this patient met Level 3.1 criteria for RTC services. ASAM criteria focuses on six dimensions to determine the appropriate level of care, which includes: (1) intoxication and withdrawal potential; (2) biomedical conditions; (3) emotional, behavioral and cognitive conditions; (4) readiness to change; (5) relapse, continued use, or continued problem potential; and (6) recovery environment. This criterion was met.For dimension 2, the patient did not have acute medical problems. The patient’s biomedical problems were stable and did not require 24-hour medical or nurse monitoring. This criterion was met.For dimension 3, the patient had a long mental health history and diagnoses of bipolar disorder, depression, and anxiety. He reported only sleeping for three to four hours a night due to nightmares. The records noted significant psychiatric symptoms, such as grandiosity, with a strong spiritual delusion and feelings of superiority. He was on psychiatric medications but still displayed psychiatric symptoms. The records noted that the patient was often disruptive in group sessions. He was described as having antisocial behaviors and lacking insight into his behaviors. The records noted that the patient was placed in a group home at age seven due to maternal neglect and had a history of being abused as a child. The records noted that the patient had joined a cult and presented himself as a kind of teacher of philosophy, quoting the Bible and Koran out of context, which alienated him from his peers. The patient was also noted as verbalizing his superiority of other races and women. The records noted a history of  driving under the influence, lying, infidelity, and gambling when using substances. The patient’s mental status, including emotional stability and cognitive functioning, was assessed as sufficiently stable to permit the patient to participate in the therapeutic interventions provided at this level of care and to benefit from treatment, and the patient’s symptoms and functional limitations, when considered in the context of the patient’s home environment, are sufficiently severe that the patient is assessed as not likely to maintain mental stability and/or abstinence if treatment is provided in a nonresidential setting. This criterion was met.For dimension 4, the patient was noted as being disruptive during group sessions, not taking responsibility for his actions, and being ambivalent about making changes that would support his sobriety. The patient required a 24-hour structured milieu to promote treatment progress and recovery, because motivating interventions had failed in the past and such interventions were assessed as not likely to succeed in an outpatient setting. This criterion was met.For dimension 5, the patient has a history of multiple treatment episodes without being able to remain clean and sober for any length of time. He was unemployed and reported being terminated due to substance use. He did not have a definite plan for what he wanted to do when he left treatment. The records noted that the patient had poor coping skills to aid him in staying away from drugs and alcohol and was at high risk of relapse. The patient demonstrated limited coping skills to address relapse triggers and urges and/or deteriorating mental functioning. The patient was thus in imminent danger of relapse, with dangerous emotional, behavioral, or cognitive consequences, and needed 24-hour structure to aid in applying recovery and coping skills. This criterion was met.For dimension 6, the patient lived with roommates but had been staying in a motel as he wanted to keep his substance use hidden from his roommates. The services at issue were not primarily for the economic benefit of the health care service plan and subscribers or for the convenience of the patient, treating physician, or other health care provider. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: The patient has requested reimbursement for residential treatment center (RTC) services (ASAM 3.5). For dimension 1, the patient did not report any withdrawal symptoms during the RTC admission. This criterion was met. For dimension 2, the patient has a history of acute medical problems. However, during this RTC admission, the patient did not reportedly experience any acute medical problems. This criterion was met.For dimension 3, the patient was able to participate in treatment despite her mental health problems. The patient was diagnosed with major depressive disorder and generalized anxiety disorder. She was started on Lexapro for anxiety and depression and Trazodone for insomnia, but she experienced anger and irritability from Lexapro. During a follow-up appointment, the patient’s mediations were changed to Wellbutrin and Seroquel, and the patient subsequently reported that Seroquel made her tired and unmotivated. The patient was also treated with gabapentin. During the RTC admission, the providers described the patient’s mood as depressed and anxious. The patient occasionally refused to go to individual therapy. The patient’s mental status was assessed as sufficiently stable to permit the patient to participate in the therapeutic interventions provided at this level of care and to benefit from treatment. In addition, the patient’s psychiatric condition was stabilizing. However, despite her best efforts, the patient was unable to control her use of substances with attendant probability of imminent danger. The resulting level of dysfunction was so severe that it precluded the patient’s participation in a less structured and intensive level of care. This criterion was met.For dimension 4, the patient asked to leave treatment once and the provider talked her into staying. The providers noted that the patient occasionally would not share during group and she sometimes refused her individual therapy sessions. The patient was looking into sober living, but she reported to staff that her child was in the hospital and she had to leave treatment. The patient’s providers tried to talk the patient into staying but she insisted on leaving without a discharge plan in place. On review the available records the patient demonstrated passive or active opposition to addressing the severity of her mental addiction or problem and did not recognize the need for treatment. Such continued substance use or inability to follow through with mental health treatment posed a danger of harm to self or others. However, assessment indicated that treatment interventions available at level 3.5 may have increased the patient’s degree of readiness to change. This criterion was met.For dimension 5, the patient reported that she was unfamiliar with the 12-step program but was previously in treatment. The patient was able to remain clean and sober for two months, then relapsed with methamphetamines, alcohol, and benzodiazepines three to four times a week. The patient previously overdosed on fentanyl and was able to stop using heroin. The patient was often uncooperative in treatment and asked to leave against the providers’ advice. The records document that the patient did not recognize relapse triggers and lacked insight into the benefits of continuing care and was therefore not committed to treatment. The patient’s continued substance use posed an imminent danger of harm to self or others in the absence of 24-hour monitoring and structured support. This criterion was met.For dimension 6, the patient was administratively discharged, without a discharge plan documented. The patient’s treatment plan included possible sober living or step down to partial hospitalization program (PHP) or intensive outpatient program (IOP). If the patient returned to her usual place of living, the relapse risk was high due to triggers and people. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: An enrollee has requested authorization and coverage for Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) Therapy.At issue in this case is whether the requested Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) Therapy is medically necessary to treat the patient’s mental health or substance use disorder, as defined in Health and Safety Code section 1374.72(a)(3)(A).California Health and Safety Code section 1374.72(a)(3)(A) states that, “Medically necessary treatment of a mental health or substance use disorder” means a service or product addressing the specific needs of that patient, for the purpose of preventing, diagnosing, or treating an illness, injury, condition, or its symptoms, including minimizing the progression of that illness, injury, condition, or its symptoms, in a manner that is all of the following:(i)	In accordance with the generally accepted standards of mental health and substance use disorder care.(ii)	Clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration.(iii)	Not primarily for the economic benefit of the health care service plan and subscribers or for the convenience of the patient, treating physician, or other health care provider.Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) psychotherapy is a well-established psychotherapy modality for the treatment of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) and symptoms related to past trauma in adults. The American Psychological Association (APA) guideline development panel (GDP) conditionally recommends the use of EMDR for posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) in adults. Practice guidelines developed by the Department of Veterans Affairs and the Department of Defense for the management of PTSD and acute stress disorder recommend individual, manualized trauma-focused psychotherapies that have a primary component of exposure and/or cognitive restructuring, including EMDR, for patients with PTSD.In this case, the patient has a history of significant trauma with mood and anxiety symptoms progressing from that trauma. The patient is also noted to have the comorbidity of traumatic brain injury (TBI). While EMDR is a well-established and recommended modality for the treatment of PTSD, there is not much available literature regarding the use of EMDR in patients with TBI. Furthermore, the submitted medical records reflect that the patient experienced physical symptoms that worsened with full EMDR. One provider recommended that the patient hold off Eye Movement Desensitization and Reprocessing (EMDR) Therapy due to concerns that it could make the patient’s vestibular issues worse and cause headache and vomiting. Another provider noted that the patient was unable to tolerate full EMDR due to “brain agitation” that the patient reported when practicing Bilateral Stimulation (BLS) during an appointment. At that time, the patient was advised to start working on a tapping, flash technique in psychotherapy that might lead up to EMDR therapy. Therefore, until the patient’s neurological symptoms are noted to be under better control, EMDR is not a clinically appropriate treatment for the patient’s PTSD and associated symptoms. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: The enrollee has requested reimbursement for Residential Treatment Center (ASAM 3.5) level of care services. Findings:  The physician reviewer found that California Health and Safety Code section 1374.72(a)(3)(A) states that “Medically necessary treatment of a mental health or substance use disorder” means a service or product addressing the specific needs of that patient, for the purpose of preventing, diagnosing, or treating an illness, injury, condition, or its symptoms, including minimizing the progression of that illness, injury, condition, or its symptoms, in a manner that is all of the following:(i)	In accordance with the generally accepted standards of mental health and substance use disorder care.(ii)	Clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration.(iii)	Not primarily for the economic benefit of the health care service plan and subscribers or for the convenience of the patient, treating physician, or other health care provider.American Society of Addiction Medicine (ASAM) criteria focus on six dimensions to determine the appropriate level of care.For dimension 1 - Acute Intoxication and/or Withdrawal Potential. This dimension assesses the patient’s current and past use of substances, as well as their history of withdrawal. In this case, the patient completed detoxification and refused Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) including both methadone and Suboxone for his opiate addiction. Records reflect that the patient had no acute withdrawal symptoms.For dimension 2 - Biomedical Conditions and Complications. This dimension explores a patient’s medical needs and health history. In this case, the patient was not being treated for any acute medical issues and was healthy.For dimension 3 - Emotional, Behavioral, or Cognitive Conditions and Complications. In this case, the patient was diagnosed with obsessive-compulsive disorder at the age of six, when he presented with hand washing and list making. More recently, the patient’s symptoms were described as mild on medications and involved `looping thinking.` Records indicate that prior to his relapse, the patient was stable on the psychiatric medications Prozac and Abilify and had only mild symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder. During the month that the patient relapsed, he was noncompliant with his obsessive-compulsive disorder medications, and he was placed back on his medications when he entered treatment. The patient reported that a job change had increased his obsessive-compulsive disorder symptoms, which he indicated had contributed to his recent relapse. For the time period under review, the patient was psychiatrically stable and was not psychotic or a danger to himself or others. The patient did not meet level 3.5 criteria for this dimension.For dimension 4 - Readiness to Change. This dimension determines a patient’s willingness and readiness to change their substance use. In this case, the patient reported that he was ready to change his life, as he did not want to die. Prior to his relapse, the patient had two years clean and sober. According to his records, the patient had been doing well on his psychiatric medications and was enjoying life. The patient did not meet level 3.5 criteria for this dimension.For dimension 5 - Relapse, Continued use, or Continued Problem Potential. This dimension assesses a patient’s individual needs that can influence their potential to relapse. In this case, there were no reports of severe cravings in the patient’s chart. Notes indicate that the patient refused Medication-Assisted Treatment (MAT) for his opiate addiction including Suboxone or methadone. The patient had been using drugs for one month and alcohol for one week after a period of two years of sobriety. The patient reported that he was motivated to stay clean and sober, as drug and alcohol use had interfered with his relationships with his family and girlfriend, and he had stopped going to his job. The patient did not meet level 3.5 criteria for this dimension.For dimension 6 - Recovery Environment. This dimension assesses how a patient’s living situation can help or hinder their recovery. In this case, the patient was being discharged to sober living, as his mother would not take him back into her home until he completed treatment. Records reflect that the patient’s mother and girlfriend were supportive of his recovery, and he had been clean and sober for two years, so he had good coping skills that would help him avoid relapse. The patient would have the support of sober living and the community recovery environment. The patient did not meet level 3.5 criteria for this dimension for the time period under review.Using the ASAM level 3.5 criteria, the patient did not meet all six dimensional criteria for medical necessity and therefore did not qualify for ASAM Level 3.5 treatment for the time period under review. The patient’s scores under the six ASAM criteria consider the specific needs of the patient for the purpose of treating their illness and its symptoms. The ASAM criteria for determining the appropriate level of care are consistent with generally accepted standards of mental health, and they provide determinations that are clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration. The ASAM criteria are also free from consideration of the economic benefit of the health care service plan and subscribers or for the convenience of the patient, treating physician, or other health care provider. Accordingly, the Residential Treatment Center (ASAM 3.5) level of care services provided during the time period under review were not medically necessary as defined in Health and Safety Code section 1374.72(a)(3)(A).Final Result: The reviewer determined that the services at issue were not medically necessary as defined in Health and Safety Code section 1374.72(a)(3)(A). This instrument is a standardized tool used to determine the intensity of services needed for children and adolescents, 6-18 years of age, presenting with psychiatric, substance use, medical and/or developmental concerns. Using CALOCUS-CASII, providers score patients on a scale of 1-5 using a six-pronged Dimensional Rating System. The six dimensions include: (1) risk of harm; (2) functional status; (3) co-occurrence of developmental, medical, substance use and psychiatric conditions; (4) recovery environment (a. stressors and b. supports); (5) resiliency and response to services; and (6) engagement. The composite score is then used to determine the level of care needed. Applying the CALOCUS-CASII framework, the patient met the criteria for RTC services. For dimension 1, the patient was at serious risk of harm (score 4) due to a history of attempting suicide on more than one occasion. The patient surreptitiously obtained items to engage in self-harm and she reportedly self-harmed on multiple occasions during the RTC admission. The patient also threatened to elope from RTC several times. There is documentation of current suicidal ideation with a past history of carrying out such behavior. There is also indication or report of significant impulsivity and poor judgment that was significantly endangering to self. For dimension 2, the patient demonstrated serious functional impairment (score 4) since she struggled to manage her emotions as evidenced by punching walls and throwing food items around her room. The patient was often rude to peers and staff, intermittently argumentative, and she struggled to comply with basic expectations. The patient’s participation and effort in school was poor. The patient showed serious deterioration of interpersonal interactions with consistent conflict or otherwise disrupted interactions with others, which may include impulsive or abusive behaviors. For dimension 3, the patient has significant co-occurrence of conditions (score 3) given her history of polysubstance use and insomnia. Both substance use and insomnia can exacerbate mood and anxiety symptoms and conversely, anxiety and depression can exacerbate insomnia and contribute to ongoing issues of self-medicating with substance use. There is evidence of medical conditions that may have adversely affected, or been affected by, the presenting condition. In addition, substance abuse was present, with significant adverse effect on functioning and the presenting condition. For dimension 4A, the patient’s recovery environment was highly stressful (score 4). The provider noted that the patient was sexually assaulted, and the case was being prosecuted. The patient’s parents are divorced, and she has longstanding and ongoing conflict with her parents. Her parents have been unable to manage her significant acting out behaviors. The records document serious disruption of family milieu. For dimension 4B, the patient’s recovery environment provided limited support (score 3). The records document that the patient’s parents were supportive of the patient. However, community resources only partially compensated for unmet emotional and educational needs. For dimension 5, the patient exhibited poor resiliency and response to treatment (score 4). The patient demonstrated frequent evidence of innate vulnerability under stress and difficulty resuming progress toward expected developmental level. Prior treatment has included outpatient psychotherapy, psychiatric care including psychiatric medications, an intensive outpatient program, two partial hospitalization programs, residential treatment including a wilderness program, and a psychiatric hospitalization. For dimension 6, the patient exhibited minimal engagement in services (score 4) due to the patient’s disruptive and argumentative behaviors during groups, and intermittent struggles to participate in groups and milieu activities. The patient’s engagement in family and individual therapy sessions was inconsistent. The patient did not accept age-appropriate responsibility for their role in the development, perpetuation, and consequences of the problem. These findings give the patient a composite score of 26, which is consistent with Level 5 medically monitored residence-based services. Per CALOCUS-CASII, the patient’s scores of 4 for risk of harm and functional status also supports treatment at Level 5. Moreover, the RTC services were in accordance with the generally accepted standards of mental health and substance use disorder care, clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration, and not primarily for the convenience of the patient or provider. For these reasons, the RTC services were medically necessary for treatment of this patient. The patient qualified for PHP services based on meeting these criteria. For dimension 3, the patient has been diagnosed with anxiety disorder and depression. It was noted by the treatment team that the patient uses opioids to cope with depression. Problems in dimension 3 are not necessary for admission to a Level 2.5 program. For dimension 4, the patient struggled with consistent participation in the treatment milieu and he frequently left groups before dismissal. The patient misused his suboxone and was discharged from the program. The patient’s perspective and lack of impulse control inhibited his ability to make behavioral changes without repeated, structured, clinically directed motivational interventions. The six dimensions include: (1) risk of harm; (2) functional status; (3) co-occurrence of developmental, medical, substance use and psychiatric conditions; (4) recovery environment (a. stressors and b. supports); (5) resiliency and response to services; and (6) engagement. The composite score is then used to determine the level of care needed. During the period under review, the patient was noted to struggle with passive suicidal ideation and ongoing urges to self-harm, particularly in response to stressors. This indicates significant risk of harm. In terms of functional status, the records support a score of 3. Records describe the patient as struggling to complete schoolwork due to poor focus and concentration resulting from her mental health issues. The patient was also noted to struggle with social isolation and completing chores at home. This is indicative of moderate functional impairment. Furthermore, mother struggles with emotion dysregulation and alcohol use. The patient’s provider has recommended treatment with parent-child interaction therapy, CDI, VDI and Fad-ins with community exposure. The authors found that in-person with the patient for 12-16 weeks yielded gains that were largely maintained in a five-year follow up. Catchpole and colleagues reported on a cohort of 33 children with selective mutism who were treated with parent-child interaction therapy principles and behavioral techniques. The authors reported that, “Results showed significant and large gains in speaking behaviors across contexts from pre- to post-treatment.” Moreover, the requested therapy services are in accordance with the generally accepted standards of mental health and substance use disorder care, clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration, and not primarily for the convenience of the patient or provider. Given this support, the requested weekly parent-child interaction therapy, weekly CDI, weekly VDI, weekly Fad-ins, and community exposure is medically necessary for treatment of this patient. Final Result: The reviewer determined that the requested services are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. Therefore, the Health Plan’s denial should be overturned. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary:  The parents of an enrollee has requested reimbursement and prospective authorization and coverage for all or any of the intensive outpatient program (IOP) services provided at Insight Treatment Program from 8/03/21, going forward.At issue is whether all or any of the IOP services provided at Insight Treatment Program from 8/03/21, going forward were and are medically necessary to treat the patient’s medical condition as defined in Health and Safety code section 1374(a)(3)(A) set forth below. “Medically necessary treatment of a mental health or substance use disorder” means a service or product addressing the specific needs of that patient, for the purpose of preventing, diagnosing, or treating an illness, injury, condition, or its symptoms, including minimizing the progression of that illness, injury, condition, or its symptoms, in a manner that is all of the following: (i) in accordance with the generally accepted standards of mental health and substance use disorder care; (ii) clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration; (iii) not primarily for the economic benefit of the health care service plan and subscribers or for the convenience of the patient, treating physician, or other health care provider.The Child and Adolescent Level of Care Utilization System (CALOCUS) provides a framework for determining the clinically appropriate level of care for a child or adolescent in mental health treatment. Using CALOCUS, providers score patients on a scale of 1-5 using a six-pronged Dimensional Rating System. The six dimensions include: (1) risk of harm; (2) functional status; (3) medical, addictive and psychiatric comorbidity; (4) recovery environment (a. stressors and b. supports); (5) treatment and recovery history; and (6) engagement. The composite score is then used to determine the level of care needed.With regard to risk of harm, the records support a score of 3. The patient has persistent passive suicidal ideation, a relapse with self-harming behavior, and had been restricting food intake. The patient also experienced panic attacks at school and contacted her therapist for support.In terms of functional status, the records support a score of 3. The patient has difficulty communicating with her family, as well as the gains she achieved while participating in the highly structured environment of the IOP program. The patient has had reports of several weeks of food restriction, which demonstrates moderate functional impairment. With regard to comorbidity, the records support a score of 1. The patient does not have reports of substance abuse, medical, or developmental disorders.In terms of level of stress of the recovery environment, the records support a score of 2. The patient has stress and anxiety related to returning to in-person school and navigating social and family relationships as well as academic pressures. With regard to level of support of the recovery environment, the records support a score of 2. The patient is actively participating in treatment.These findings give the patient a composite score of 16. At this level of care, treatment intensity ranges from one hour every four weeks, to up to two hours per week. The IOP level of care being requested cannot be justified when the CALOCUS criteria are applied to the clinical records provided. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: The patient’s parent has requested reimbursement and prospective authorization and coverage for individual parent-child interaction therapy (PCIT) services provided by an independent provider. At issue in this case is whether the individual PCIT services were and/or are medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s mental health or substance use disorder as defined in Health and Safety Code section 1374(a)(3)(A). “Medically necessary treatment of a mental health or substance use disorder” means a service or product addressing the specific needs of that patient, for the purpose of preventing, diagnosing, or treating an illness, injury, condition, or its symptoms, including minimizing the progression of that illness, injury, condition, or its symptoms, in a manner that is all of the following: (i) In accordance with the generally accepted standards of mental health and substance use disorder care. (ii) Clinically appropriate in terms of type, frequency, extent, site, and duration. (iii) Not primarily for the economic benefit of the health care service plan and subscribers or for the convenience of the patient, treating physician, or other health care provider.PCIT is an evidence-based approach intended to treat disruptive behavior problems in children two to seven years of age. The goals of PCIT are to encourage warm and secure parent-child relationships, increase child compliance, and decrease disruptive behaviors (Lieneman, et al.). Based on the patient’s challenging behaviors and age, PCIT would be an appropriate and medically necessary intervention. Per the submitted documentation, the Health Plan offered the patient’s parents group PCIT, but the parents declined. They were also offered individual and family therapy. In their independent medical review application/complaint form, the patient’s parents stated that group PCIT is not evidence-based.  Although PCIT was initially developed to work with the individual caregiver and child, PCIT has been successfully adapted to a group format. Adapting PCIT to a group strategy is considered by many to be an innovative strategy to reach more families with the additional benefit of peer support. Nieter and colleagues noted, “Although PCIT is typically delivered in outpatient clinic-based settings with individual families, research has demonstrated positive outcomes when the model is applied in a group-based format.” The authors reported that when comparing “individual PCIT to group PCIT, significant improvements were noted in child conduct problems, parenting stress, and children’s adaptive functioning in both formats.” When practiced with fidelity to the PCIT model, group PCIT includes the same didactic sessions at the beginning of treatment as individual PCIT and coaching sessions are similar in structure and content to individual PCIT. Therefore, individual PCIT services were not and are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s mental health or substance use disorder as defined in Health and Safety Code section 1374(a)(3)(A).Final Result: The reviewer determined that the services at issue were not and are not medically necessary for treatment of the patient’s medical condition. Therefore, the Health Plan’s denial should be upheld. The six dimensions include: (1) risk of harm; (2) functional status; (3) medical, addictive and psychiatric comorbidity; (4) recovery environment (a. stressors and b. supports); (5) treatment and recovery history; and (6) engagement. When the patient initially presented to receive IOP services, she had significant impairment in her personal hygiene and self-care. The patient made improvements during the month that she received IOP services, but these gains have only been maintained while participating in treatment in this structured setting, and she immediately destabilized again upon removal of this structured setting. This qualifies the patient for moderate impairment in this dimension. [Score 3 – Moderate Impairment]For dimension 3 – Comorbidity. The patient is able to access help from her supports, if needed, though they have incomplete ability to participate in treatment and in supporting the patient due to the pandemic. [Score 3 – Limited Engagement and Recovery]Thus, the patient has a composite score of 19, which corresponds with a Level 3: High Intensity Community Based Services level of care, or IOP. Nature of Statutory Criteria/Case Summary: An enrollee has requested authorization and coverage for ongoing cognitive processing therapy (CPT).Cognitive processing therapy (CPT) is a specific treatment approach developed for post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which requires specialized training. In their 2017 clinical practice guidelines for the treatment of PTSD, the American Psychological Association (APA) strongly recommends the following approaches: cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT), CPT, cognitive therapy, and prolonged exposure therapy. According to the Veterans Administration (VA) National Center for PTSD, `Although CPT was originally developed as a 12-session protocol, it is now administered over a variable number of sessions, depending on patient needs. This change stemmed from a study by Galovski et al. (2012) which found that ending therapy based on patient progress yielded better results than using a proscribed number of sessions—by the end of the study, 92% of the participants who had variable length CPT no longer had a diagnosis of PTSD.` Per APA guidelines for PTSD, individuals’ post-trauma reactions show great variability, ranging from those that are highly resilient--with little or no emotional distress-- to those that are relatively mild and short-term, to those that are major, chronic, and highly debilitating. In their 2012 study, Galovski and colleagues concluded that it is possible that living with PTSD for extended periods of time (irrespective of current age of the client) may result in more diffuse distress, overall role impairment, and subsequent deficits in functioning. A chronic PTSD clinical presentation may present additional challenges in therapy, requiring a longer course of treatment. Elevated depression prior to therapy also emerged as a significant predictor of length of treatment. The presence of elevated depression prior to treatment may portend a longer road to recovery. Their study found that continuing the course of CPT is warranted if resolution of PTSD and depressive symptoms has not been fully achieved by the end of the standard 12-session protocol.In this case, the patient had suffered with symptoms for years prior to treatment. The patient has requested reimbursement for residential treatment center (RTC) services. The American Academy of Child and Adolescent Psychiatry and the American Association of Community Psychiatrists Child and Adolescent Level of Care Utilization System (CALOCUS) provides a reliable framework for determining the appropriate level of care for adolescents needing mental health treatment. Using CALOCUS, providers score patients on a scale of 1-5 using a six-pronged Dimensional Rating System. The six dimensions include: (1) risk of harm; (2) functional status; (3) developmental, medical, substance use and psychiatric comorbidity; (4) recovery environment (a. stressors and b. supports); (5) treatment and recovery history; and (6) engagement. The composite score is then used to determine the level of care needed. Applying the CALOCUS framework, this patient met the criteria for RTC services. For dimension 1, the patient was at serious risk of harm (score 4) due his assaultive behavior and elopement from the previous RTC, as well as anger outbursts and defiance towards staff at the second RTC. There was indication or report of significant impulsivity and/or physical or sexual aggression, with poor judgment and insight, and that were significantly endangering to others. For dimension 2, the patient demonstrated serious functional impairment (score 4) given his serious deterioration of interpersonal interactions with consistent conflict or otherwise disrupted interactions with others, which included impulsive or abusive behaviors. The patient was discharged from the previous RTC after assaulting a peer and running away. He also struggled with interactions with peers and staff at the second RTC. For dimension 3, the patient has no comorbidities (score 1). No evidence of medical illness, substance abuse, developmental disability, or psychiatric disturbances apart from the presenting condition. For dimension 4A, the patient’s recovery environment was moderately stressful (score 3) considering his multiple moves between home and various treatment settings, which supports disruption of family and social milieu. For dimension 4B, the patient’s recovery environment was supportive (score 2) due to his mother’s active participation in treatment. The patient’s family were willing and able to participate in treatment if requested to do so and had capacity to effect needed changes. For dimension 5, the patient exhibited poor resiliency and response to treatment (score 4). The records document that previous treatment has not achieved complete remission of symptoms or optimal control of symptoms even with intensive and repeated exposure to treatment. The patient has persistent symptoms despite an extensive treatment history at various levels of care, including RTC. For dimension 6, the patient was incompletely engaged in treatment (score 3) given his tendency to blame others rather than accept responsibility for his own actions and their consequences. The patient minimized and rationalized distressing behaviors and consequences. This gives the patient a composite score of 21, which is consistent with Level 4 medically monitored community-based services. Per CALOCUS, the patient’s score of 4 for risk of harm supports an indication for Level 5 medically monitored residence-based services. Furthermore, the patient qualified for Level 5C long-term medically monitored residence-based services since his symptoms were “persistent despite extensive and intensive treatment exposure.” These facilities will provide intensive treatment as described for all Level 5 programs and the length of stay varies from two months to one year.
